video_title: Lawfare Daily: Far-Right Gains and a Political Reckoning in Germany
gist: A Brookings analyst of the US and Europe walks through the AfD's near-44% showing in the September 6 Saxony-Anhalt state election, arguing the party is materially more radical than Le Pen's or Meloni's parties, is anti-EU, anti-euro and functionally anti-NATO with a stated preference for close ties to Russia and China, and that a German party ban is legally available but politically self-defeating. The stakes are framed as European rather than German: with two more state elections on September 20, a wobbling Merz coalition, Le Pen polling well for 2027 and daily Russian shadow-warfare incidents against European infrastructure, the guest argues the stability of Europe now turns on whether German centrist parties can deliver credible governance.

themes.theme: AfD origins and current electoral ceiling

insights.claim: Germany's AfD was founded in 2013 as an anti-euro party by libertarian German professors who believed the common European currency was destroying the German economy, and its name mocks Angela Merkel's habitual line that 'there is no alternative.'
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: The party's founding DNA is monetary-union scepticism, not just migration, so any AfD accretion of national power carries direct euro-redenomination and EU-cohesion tail risk rather than purely social policy risk.

insights.claim: For its first five years the AfD never cleared roughly 4-5% in elections, and its breakout came only after the migration wave the guest dates to 2018, when Angela Merkel opened Germany's borders to Syrian and other refugees.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: The AfD's support is event-triggered rather than structural-from-birth, which means future migration or capacity shocks in Europe are the observable catalysts for further far-right repricing of European political risk.

insights.claim: The AfD took almost 44% of the vote in the September 6 state election in Saxony-Anhalt, a state of 2.1 million people, while polling only around 20-21% nationally.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: The gap between a regional near-majority and a national fifth is the key number to watch: national power still requires either a doubling of support or a coalition partner, so headline state results overstate near-term federal policy risk.
insights.quote: the AFD polls at around 20 21% nationally

insights.claim: The guest argues three-quarters to four-fifths of Germans remain horrified by the AfD, so the party's path to national power depends on centrist failure rather than on majority conversion.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Watch centrist-party performance metrics, not AfD rallies, as the leading indicator for German political discontinuity.

insights.claim: The AfD is treated as too extreme to associate with by Europe's other national-populist parties, including Marine Le Pen's Rassemblement National, Giorgia Meloni's Italian government, and the UK's Reform and Restore parties.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Investors should not price the AfD off the Meloni template of a far-right party that normalized in office; the guest's explicit claim is that the German case is a different and more disruptive category.

insights.claim: The AfD has imposed rigid internal discipline on a party that used to fracture publicly at conventions, which the guest reads as evidence it is seriously pursuing national power and will stop at very little to get there.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Loss of the party's historic self-sabotage removes the main mechanism that previously capped its growth, raising the probability that its national polling trend continues rather than mean-reverts.
insights.quote: the AFD has developed an absolutely astounding internal discipline

insights.claim: Germany's 1949 basic law, drafted with heavy American input including German Jewish constitutional lawyers who had fled the Nazis, embeds 'militant democracy' provisions that make the bill of rights and the parliamentary federal structure immune to constitutional amendment and permit banning unconstitutional parties.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Germany has legal circuit breakers the US lacks, which caps the worst-case constitutional scenario but also means any AfD advance triggers a contested legal process rather than a clean transfer of power.

insights.claim: The party-ban provision has de facto been used only twice, both in the 1950s, and subsequent constitutional court rulings set the bar for a ban very high.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: The base rate for an actual ban is extremely low; positioning around headlines about banning the AfD is likely to be positioning around an event that does not happen.
insights.quote: it allows for the ban of unconstitutional parties but that has de facto only happened twice in in the in the 1950s

insights.claim: A ban would require initiation by parliament and adjudication by the constitutional court, and the guest argues the stronger the AfD becomes the weaker the democratic legitimacy of banning it, a paradox she calls the trap of the provision.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: The legal off-ramp closes precisely as the political risk rises, so the tail scenario cannot be assumed to be legally contained.

insights.claim: German domestic intelligence has finally classified the AfD's state chapters as right-wing extremist in five of Germany's 16 states, while the federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution's nationwide classification is under court challenge and currently suspended.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
entities: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution
insights.so_what: The pending court ruling on the national extremist designation is a concrete, dateable German political-risk catalyst, and the guest expects the court to have no trouble upholding it.

insights.claim: The core legal case against the AfD rests on intelligence assessments that the party holds an ethnonationalist conception of German identity and citizenship that contradicts the foundational principles of the constitution's bill of rights.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: This is the single legal finding that would anchor any future ban proceeding or coalition exclusion, making it the document trail to track.
insights.quote: the AFD has an ethnationalist view of German identity and German citizenship that is against the foundational principles of the German constitution's bill of rights

insights.claim: An AfD legislator named at a party rally about two weeks earlier said Germany needs only 60 million people, which against a population of 83 million implies removing roughly 23 million German citizens with foreign roots, a group that includes Soviet Jews who arrived after 1991 and post-1945 expellees.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Roughly 25% of Germany's population has foreign roots and its health and elder-care systems depend on immigrant staff, so any serious move toward this program would be a labor-supply shock to German services, not just a civil-rights event.

insights.claim: The guest rejects the standard immigration explanation for AfD strength in the east, noting that East Germany and Saxony-Anhalt have some of the lowest immigration levels in Germany while immigrant concentration is far higher in the west.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: If far-right support is not actually driven by local immigration levels, then migration-restriction policy will not defuse it, and political risk persists even if European border policy tightens.
insights.quote: East Germany and indeed Saxony Enheld has some of the lowest levels of immigration of all of Germany

insights.claim: The guest's own explanatory framework is 'systems overload': mature, institutionally solid Western democracies are struggling simultaneously with globalization, economic interdependence and aggressive outside interference from Russia, China and to some degree the Trump administration.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: A reusable model for pricing political risk across developed markets: the driver is cumulative institutional strain, so the same instability premium should be expected in multiple Western democracies at once rather than in isolated cases.
insights.quote: we are seeing in all western societies a form of systems overload

insights.claim: The guest explicitly rejects the Steve Bannon 'culture is upstream of politics' explanation for German far-right support as tempting but not compelling.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Analysts using culture-war framing to forecast European elections are, on this view, using the wrong model; institutional-capacity and delivery metrics are the better predictors.

insights.claim: East Germans experienced 12 years of Nazism plus an additional 44 years of Soviet-backed communist rule and pervasive civil-society surveillance, producing what the guest calls a mixture of vulnerability and affinity toward Russia that the AfD exploits.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Pro-Russia sentiment in eastern Germany is structural and decades deep, so sanctions cohesion and energy policy toward Russia face a durable domestic constituency against them.

insights.claim: The guest traces current AfD support to an abdication of public order 35 years ago, when neo-Nazi gangs marauded in the countryside around Berlin in the early 1990s and Berlin authorities dismissed attacks on refugee homes as isolated incidents that would soon pass.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: If the roots are 35 years deep, mean-reversion in German far-right support is unlikely on any investment-relevant horizon.

insights.claim: Germany's political elites refused for a long time to admit that global disruption would threaten German democratic institutions, a denial the guest says took Germans longer to shed than their central and eastern European neighbors.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Suggests German policy responses will continue to lag events, which argues for assuming slower, later German adjustment than consensus in crisis scenarios.

insights.claim: The US vice president used the Munich Security Conference to lay out a vision of a transatlantic civilizational alliance of right-wing ethnonationalist parties and met AfD co-chair Alice Vital there, but the guest says subsequent official contact has been largely backbencher-to-backbencher.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: The headline endorsement overstates the operational depth of US-AfD ties, so a US-backed AfD normalization is less imminent than the rhetoric implies.

insights.claim: After the Saxony-Anhalt result the AfD received congratulations from the US president, Elon Musk and former Berlin ambassador Richard Grenell, but pointedly not from the vice president, which the guest reads as both sides deciding to tone things down.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: The pattern of who congratulates and who stays silent is a cheap real-time gauge of how far the US administration intends to push destabilization of European centrist governments.

insights.claim: Large parts of the AfD, especially its East German base, are deeply anti-American with a real emotional attachment to Russia and sincere acceptance of ties with China, which limits how far the party can align with Washington.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: An ascendant AfD is not a reliable US ally but a vector for Russian and Chinese influence inside the EU's largest economy, which is the more consequential scenario for sanctions, export controls and NATO cohesion.

insights.claim: The attack on Iran was profoundly unpopular in Europe not only among centrist voters but also on the hard right, forcing AfD leadership to walk back its pro-American positioning.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: US military action in the Middle East measurably widens the transatlantic political gap even with Europe's nationalist right, a second-order effect to watch after any further escalation.

insights.claim: The AfD is anti-EU and anti-euro, and the guest says it is also clearly anti-NATO while pretending otherwise because its national leadership is still hoping for American support amid ambivalent Trump administration signaling on the Western alliance.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: The party's stated NATO position should be discounted as tactical; the underlying preference is a nationalist security policy with close Russia and China ties, which is the scenario to stress-test for European defense and sovereign spreads.
insights.quote: that the AfD would prefer to have a a national security policy based on nationalism and dominance I think is is perfectly clear

themes.theme: Firewall politics and CDU coalition risk

insights.claim: The CDU and the Social Democrats together once commanded 80-90% of the German federal vote and their leaderships still have not internalized that German politics is now as fragmented and polarized as everyone else's.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Strategic misreading by the governing parties makes further centrist vote erosion the base case, which sustains a German political-risk premium regardless of any single election result.

insights.claim: The firewall against coalitions with the AfD is hard and fast nationally but already fails at local and regional level in small, less populated rural areas where parties routinely cooperate with the AfD.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Normalization is happening bottom-up regardless of national declarations, so the firewall's collapse will likely be gradual and visible in municipal politics before it appears at federal level.
insights.quote: at this at the local level and at the regional level in in small and and sort of less populated rural swaththers of Germany, that firewall just simply doesn't work

insights.claim: The guest argues that if the CDU abandoned the firewall the AfD would not moderate or normalize the way other European right-wing parties have, because the AfD is further right than they are.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the common market assumption that governing responsibility tames populists, removing the soft-landing scenario from German risk models.
insights.quote: I also don't think that if the CDU abandoned the firewall and coalitioned or let itself be tolerated by the AFD that somehow the AFD would moderate or normalize. That's not going to happen.

insights.claim: The guest's prescription is that centrist parties can only save themselves by delivering good policy seen as democratic and legitimate, and she says there is plenty of evidence they have not been good at that while fixating on the AfD has itself distracted from governing.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Concrete German delivery on economic and infrastructure policy, not anti-extremist rhetoric, is the variable to track for whether the political risk premium compresses.
insights.quote: the only way they can save themselves is by is basically by making by making good policy

insights.claim: Two more state elections fall on September 20 in the city-state of Berlin and in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on the Baltic coast, and the guest expects the chancellor's CDU to get hammered again, feeding speculation that he could be forced out by his own party.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: A dated, near-term binary event for German coalition stability, with a further leg of risk if a leadership challenge follows.

insights.claim: Replacing the chancellor mid-term is constitutionally possible and has happened four times in German history, but the guest has recently changed her view and now thinks changing horses in midstream would fail and only strengthen the AfD.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: A German leadership change should be read as an escalation of instability rather than a resolution of it, which argues against relief-rally positioning on a chancellor swap.
insights.quote: changing horses in midstream is is not going to work and in fact will only strengthen the AFD

themes.theme: Europe under siege and the stakes for markets

insights.claim: AfD co-chair Alice Vital said days before recording that an AfD-led national government would end all support for Ukraine and demand repayment of all support provided over the past nearly five years.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Germany is a principal underwriter of Ukraine, so this is the sharpest single articulation of what an AfD government would mean for Ukrainian financing, European defense budgets and the credibility of EU support commitments.
insights.quote: an AfDled national government would not just end all support for Ukraine, but would ask for repayment of all the support it's received in the past nearly 5 years

insights.claim: The guest describes daily shadow warfare against Europe, citing sabotage of the entire Dutch railway network that day, weaponized drones in Lithuania that forced the closure of Vilnius airport, and a Russian ship firing flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Hybrid attacks on European transport, aviation and maritime assets are now a running operational and insurance cost, not an episodic tail risk.
insights.quote: Just today there was sabotage on the entire Dutch railway network.

insights.claim: The guest frames Europe as simultaneously under Russian shadow warfare, Chinese economic coercion, and a transatlantic alliance whose cultural and political premises the Trump administration questions on a weekly basis, calling the stakes higher than at any point in her adult lifetime.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Three concurrent external pressures on Europe argue for a structurally higher European risk premium and sustained defense and resilience spending regardless of the German election outcome.

insights.claim: German political instability transmits to the whole continent because of the size of the German economy and the deep labor-market and economic integration of its smaller neighbors.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: German domestic politics should be treated as a European-wide macro input rather than a national story, with contagion running through trade and labor linkages to smaller neighboring economies.
insights.quote: As Germany goes, so goes the stability of Europe socially, economically, and politically

insights.claim: The guest situates the German far-right surge inside a broader European pattern: the French apparently think Marine Le Pen might make a good president in 2027, the British have had seven prime ministers in a decade, and the British hard right is surging in the polls.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Correlated political risk across Germany, France and the UK means European political hedges are less diversifying than they look; the 2027 French presidential cycle is the next major dated event.

insights.claim: The chancellor campaigned and opened his term on building up European security and declaring independence from the United States, a program the host notes is now in tension with his party's eroding domestic position.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orette (host, Lawfare executive editor)
insights.so_what: European strategic autonomy and defense buildout depend on a chancellor whose domestic mandate is weakening, putting the durability of German defense commitments in question.

insights.claim: The guest's closing thesis is that the future of a stable, prosperous and secure Europe rides on whether centrist forces across Europe can persuade voters they are the most capable and legitimate source of governance at a time when stability, prosperity and security will be in very short supply.
insights.speaker: Constanza (guest, Brookings Center on the United States and Europe)
insights.so_what: Sets the frame for European political risk over the coming years: the binding constraint is centrist governing competence, and its absence is the scenario that repriced European assets would reflect.
insights.quote: the future of a stable prosperous and secure Europe rides on the ability of centrist forces to persuade their voters not just in Germany but across Europe that they are the most capable and the most legitimate source of governance
